title: America’s high achievers are doing surprisingly well on PISA
author: Brandon L. Wright
summary: Brandon Wright looks past the grim headline averages of the latest PISA results to the share of American students scoring at the advanced Levels 5 and 6. He finds that about 13 percent of U.S. fifteen-year-olds reach those levels in reading and science, roughly double the OECD averages, while math sits at the OECD average of 8 percent. The trends over the past decade are even better, with the U.S. share of top performers rising in all three subjects while the OECD average fell. Wright cautions against overselling the news: Singapore, Korea, and Japan produce advanced math students at far higher rates, over a third of U.S. students fall below baseline proficiency in math, and the U.S. has among the largest gaps between high and low performers. He also flags that the U.S. missed several PISA sampling standards. His conclusion is that the country has a substantial reservoir of academic talent and a more positive picture at the top than headlines suggested.
points: About 13 percent of U.S. students reached PISA Levels 5 or 6 in reading and science, versus roughly 6 and 7 percent across the OECD.
The U.S. ranked 4th of 89 systems in the share of top readers and 8th of 90 in science.
In math, 37 percent of Singapore's students reached the top levels compared with 8 percent in the United States.
More than one in three U.S. test takers scored below the Level 2 baseline in math, and the U.S. has the largest 90th to 10th percentile gap in reading.
U.S. results carry a caveat because the country fell short of several PISA sampling standards for participation.
quotes: The best way to determine this on PISA is to look at students scoring at Levels 5 and 6. The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)—a group of 38 mostly-affluent countries that designs and administers PISA—views such test-takers as advanced performers able to go beyond routine, age-level tasks and apply what they know to complex and unfamiliar problems.

About 13 percent of U.S. students reach those levels in reading and science, compared with roughly 6 and 7 percent across the OECD, respectively. In math, the U.S. is right around the OECD average at 8 percent.

A decade ago, the U.S. advantage over the OECD average at the high end was just 2 percentage points. Since then, the American share of top performers has risen by more than 3 percentage points, while the OECD average has fallen by about 2.
This is all good news, full stop. But it shouldn’t be oversold, and nobody should over-indulge in champagne.

In other words, the U.S. still produces advanced math students at nowhere near the rate of the world leaders, even if our comparatively large population still produces a substantial absolute number of top performers.
In fact, the United States has the largest gap between its 90th- and 10th-percentile students in reading and the second largest in science.
That leaves us with a more complicated—and more positive—picture than many PISA headlines painted. Yes, America has serious achievement problems. But there’s also a lot of good news at the high end.
